extracted.intended_audience: researchers and meta-researchers studying peer review, scientometrics, journal editors, and computational linguists performing large-scale text analysis of peer review reports
extracted.subtask_short: linguistic analysis of peer review reports
extracted.subtask_description: Large-scale empirical analysis of the linguistic characteristics of peer review reports (length, tone, sentiment, morality) using LIWC, SentimentR and Stanford CoreNLP, with mixed-model statistical controls across journals, article types and reviewer attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length of report (word count)
rubrics_metrics.description: Word count (mean and 95% CI; LIWC analysis) of peer review reports. Reports recommending accept were consistently the shortest, and reports recommending major revisions were consistently the longest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported for combinations of area of research, type of peer review and reviewer gender; social sciences and economics reports were significantly longer than medical journals; men tended to write longer reports than women; type of peer review (single- vs double-blind) did not influence length. Summary data and mixed model linear regression coefficients and residuals are provided in Supplementary file 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytical tone (LIWC)
rubrics_metrics.description: LIWC returns a standardized score between 0 and 100 for 'analytical tone'. A high score indicates a report with a logical and hierarchical style of writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical scores in this sample were high (typically between 85.0 and 91.0). Analytical tone was higher when reviewers recommended major revisions, higher when reviewers were women, and higher for single-blind peer review; no effect of area of research was detected. See Supplementary file 2 for summary data, mixed model coefficients, residuals, and example reports with high/low analytical tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clout (LIWC)
rubrics_metrics.description: LIWC returns a standardized score between 0 and 100 for 'clout', which reveals personal sensitivity towards social status, confidence or leadership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Low clout is associated with insecurities and a less confident, more tentative tone (Kacewicz et al., 2014). In this sample, reports recommending accept had highest clout, followed by minor revisions, major revisions and reject. Clout levels varied with area of research (highest in social sciences and economics). Lower clout observed when reviewers were men and when journals used single-blind review. See Supplementary file 3 for details and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity (LIWC)
rubrics_metrics.description: LIWC returns a standardized score between 0 and 100 for 'authenticity'. A high score indicates text written in a style that is honest and humble; a low score indicates deceptive or superficial style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High authenticity is defined as the use of more personal words (I-words), present tense words, and relativity words, and fewer non-personal words and modal words (Pennebaker et al., 2015). Typical scores in this sample were low (typically between 18.0 and 25.0). Authenticity was higher in social sciences and economics journals and prevalent when reviewers recommended rejection; no significant variation by reviewer gender or peer-review type. See Supplementary file 4 for summary data and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentiment / Emotional tone (multi-method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three complementary sentiment measures were used: LIWC 'emotional tone' (0–100), SentimentR (majority of scores range −1 to +1), and Stanford CoreNLP (0 to +4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All three approaches produced similar results: reports recommending accept had the highest sentiment scores, followed by minor revisions, major revisions and reject. Reports for social sciences and economics and reviews written by women had higher sentiment; no association with type of peer review. Examples and summary data are in Supplementary files 5–7. Using multiple sentiment tools served as concurrent validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: General morality (LIWC)
rubrics_metrics.description: LIWC scores for 'general morality' (mean percentage, log scale) derived from the LIWC Moral Foundations dictionary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports recommending accept had the highest general morality scores, followed by minor revisions, major revisions and reject. Differences across research areas, reviewer gender and peer review type were detected (e.g., lower proportions in social sciences and economics, when reviewers were men, and with single-blind review). Lists of most frequent words for general morality are in Supplementary file 8.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral foundations subscales (care/harm; fairness/cheating; loyalty/betrayal; authority/subversion; sanctity/degradation)
rubrics_metrics.description: LIWC was used with Moral Foundations Theory dictionaries to measure the five foundations: care/harm, fairness/cheating, loyalty/betrayal, authority/subversion, and sanctity/degradation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No clear patterns emerged for these five foundations; prevalence of these words was minimal (average scores <1%) and often part of common phrases that did not necessarily reflect moral content. Authors recommend combining qualitative and quantitative methods (including machine learning) to explore moral aspects of peer review. Supplementary file 8 lists the ten most common phrases per moral foundation; additional figures provided in Supplementary materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: LIWC dictionary counts and standardized LIWC usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of LIWC dictionaries to count words per category and return percentage scores per tone/category; authors used a standardized LIWC version.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: LIWC output is the percentage of words from a tone category in the text. The authors used the standardized version of LIWC with high Cronbach alphas and provided explanation of how LIWC measures are calculated and examples (anonymized) in the Supplementary materials. LIWC categories underpin analytical tone, clout, authenticity, emotional tone, and moral foundation measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset curation and gender determination protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures for filtering reports and determining reviewer gender prior to analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PEERE dataset was filtered (excluded reviews that included reference to manuscript revisions in the initial processing), yielding 583,365 reports; authors excluded 110,636 reports due to inability to determine reviewer gender and 260 due to missing recommendation, resulting in 472,449 reports for analysis. Gender determination used a multi-stage procedure: (1) use gender salutations when available; (2) query the gender-guesser Python package (first names, country); (3) query Gender API and accept returned gender when there were at least 62 samples with at least 57% accuracy (threshold chosen to keep misclassification rate under ~5%). This procedure produced gender assignment for 81.1% of reviewers (75.9% male, 24.1% female).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical analysis standard (mixed model linear analysis with controls)
rubrics_metrics.description: Modeling approach used to test effects on linguistic variables while controlling for confounders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each linguistic variable (analytical tone, authenticity, clout; sentiment measures; morality measures) was tested using mixed model linear analysis with reviewer recommendation, area of research, type of peer review (single- or double-blind) and reviewer gender as fixed factors, and journal, word count and article type as random factors. This controlled across-journal interactions, text length and article type. Authors followed reviewers' suggestions to present multilevel descriptions and interaction effects and caution that very large sample size can make small effects statistically significant; they therefore present standardized within-group relations and mixed-model results in Supplementary files.
